region: Carolinas, Virginia (Hurricane Florence); Dallas & San Antonio TX (TS Gordon)
weather_stated: extreme wet weather and flooding; record rain days in Dallas and San Antonio
quote: We believe the severe weather negatively affected third quarter results with a loss of some 2.5 million tons of aggregates and related flooding costs.
notes: 2.5M tons lost vs 56M tons shipped (10-Q: 'Shipments increased 5 million tons, or 10 percent, to 56 million tons') -> 2.5/58.5 = -4.3% of weather-free volume. $27M pre-tax = 7.1% of weather-free adj. EBITDA ($353.5M+$27M): profit hit ~1.7x volume hit. No rain-day deviation stated (record rain days in Dallas/San Antonio, Florence flooding Carolinas). Mgmt: work postponed; Q4 shipping days used to make it up; Jan 2019 strong on pushed 2018 work (see VMC Q2 2019 row).

weather_stated: severe weather (Florence, Gordon)
quote: We estimate that the pre-tax loss due to weather to be approximately $27 million in the quarter.
notes: -27/(353.5+27) = -7.1% of weather-free adj. EBITDA (Q3 2018 adj. EBITDA $353.5M from 10-Q). Compare -4.3% volume: profit falls ~1.7x revenue.

quote: Whatever we don't ship in 2019, we will ship in 2020. There you saw the perfect example of that's in January of this year when that work that pent up and shipped in January.
notes: Unquantified; establishes that 2018 rain-lost shipments were caught up in Jan 2019 (shipped into the following winter). See also s76117021335522069383014: 'January extremely strong with that flow through of work from 2018 pushing back'.

region: Dallas, San Antonio, Houston TX; LA, San Francisco CA; Chicago IL
weather_stated: Dallas +15 rain days, San Antonio +24, Houston +6, LA +5, SF +9; Chicago lost 22 days
quote: Dallas had another 15 days of rain. San Antonio had an increase of 24 days of rain. Houston had an increase of six days. In California, we saw L.A. up five days, San Francisco up nine days... If you look at Illinois, we lost a full month. We lost 22 days in Chicago.
notes: Extra rain days vs prior-year Q2 (not vs normal). Company shipments still +4% YoY (s77556455799814724104037); CA+TX ~30% of volume. Guidance range 3-5% -> weather roughly cost the ~1pt between top and achieved; no explicit weather estimate. Per market, +15 to +24 rain days in a ~65-workday quarter is a large deviation; aggregate effect diluted by unaffected markets.

weather_stated: markets with 17-20+ more rain days in Q3 2020 than Q3 2019 (2019 abnormally dry)
quote: We saw markets that had 17, 18, 19, 20-plus more rain days in the third quarter in 2020 than 2021. Excuse me, 2020 than 2019... you're seeing some of that work catch up in October.
notes: Unquantified shipment effect (COVID also in play). Establishes next-month catch-up.

region: Nashville/Middle Tennessee; Dallas-Fort Worth; ~70% of VMC geographies
weather_stated: Nashville 30 rain days in Q2 (lost half of shipping days); DFW double the rainfall
quote: In Q2, Nashville had 30 rain days, and it dramatically impacted shipments. Look, we lost half of our shipping days in that Middle Tennessee market. DFW had double the amount of rainfall, so we just never dried out and couldn't ship.
notes: Company shipments -5% YoY (s63711710160660696004897), mixed with soft residential demand; no clean weather estimate. Market-level: DFW rainfall +100%; Nashville ~50% of shipping days lost. Atlanta and LA had normal weather and shipped as planned. Adj. EBITDA margin still +170bp (pricing).

period_affected: 2024 Q3 (Jul: 7 of top 10 markets much wetter; Beryl, Debby, Helene)
weather_stated: 17 of 20 largest markets with more rain than prior year; four hurricanes
quote: If you look at the year, we've had 17 out of our 20 largest markets with more rain than prior year. I would call underlying demand kind of still down mid-single-digit ex-weather.
notes: Q3 shipments -10% YoY; mgmt says underlying demand down mid-single-digit, so weather ~-5pts. Includes hurricanes (not pure rain days). July: 7 of top 10 markets had significant YoY rainfall increases and daily shipments were down mid-teens (s65526486973192760547107). Adj. EBITDA only modestly down (pricing). Mgmt says 2024 volume 'pushes back' into 2025 (s62384419554005347528828).

weather_stated: significant year-over-year increases in rainfall in 7 of top 10 markets
quote: In July, seven of our top 10 markets experienced significant year-over-year increases in rainfall. The first of four hurricanes, Hurricane Beryl, made landfall in our footprint. Average daily shipments were down mid-teens for the month.
notes: 'mid-teens' recorded as -15. Underlying demand ~-5% so weather ~-10pts in that month. August ex-2 hurricane days only -4% (= underlying): rebound when dry.

quote: If I look at volume in 2025, first of all, you're going to have some push from 2024 into 2025, obviously. That volume doesn't go away. It just pushes back.
notes: Unquantified deferral statement: rain-lost 2024 shipments expected to ship the next year, not within the season. Q4 2024 call: 'we really never got out of the weather problem' in 2024 (s47697701242288514102923) - i.e. full-year 2024 volume did not catch up inside the year.

weather_stated: rainfall notched 10-year records in many key Southeast states
quote: Rainfall in the Southeast notched 10-year records in many key Vulcan states, namely Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, and the Carolinas, disrupting both our aggregate and asphalt businesses in these markets. Aggregate shipments were impacted by an estimate of 2 million tons- 3 million tons
notes: 2-3M tons vs 59.3M tons shipped (10-Q: 'Shipments decreased 1%, or 0.8 million tons, to 59.3') -> 2.5/61.8 = -4.0% (range -3.3 to -4.8). Hit 'our most profitable markets'; adj. EBITDA still +9% YoY on price; unit cash cost only +1.5%.

region: Texas (wettest Sep in 124 yrs), North/South Carolina (Florence)
weather_stated: Texas wettest September in 124 years; San Antonio ~17 in vs ~3 in normal; Florence affected 15 of 19 September selling days in Carolinas
quote: Heritage aggregate shipments adjusted for third quarter 2017 volumes from the Forsyth County, Georgia quarry we divested in April 2018 grew 4%. We estimate heritage volume growth would've been closer to 12%, absent the noted weather headwinds.
notes: 1.04/1.12-1 = -7.1% of weather-free volume for the quarter, essentially from one month (Sep): Sep is ~1/3 of the quarter, so Sep volume ~-20%. Florence: 15 of 19 selling days affected in Carolinas (~79% of the month). San Antonio rainfall ~+400% vs normal in Sep. Infrastructure shipments flat (public work most weather sensitive).

weather_stated: historically high levels of precipitation
quote: We estimate weather negatively impacted third quarter profitability by $40 million-$45 million.
notes: Midpoint $42.5M. Building materials gross profit was $288M (s60993847317065167321119) -> ~-13% of weather-free gross profit vs -7% volume: profit hit ~2x volume hit (fixed-cost under-absorption, flooded quarries). Mgmt: NC impact won't bleed into next year.

weather_stated: precipitation disrupted more than one-third of the quarter's available shipping days; Texas 11th wettest Q2 on record
deferred_or_lost: deferred (caught up within quarter; record June)
quote: Our Texas cement business delivered solid operating performance despite significant precipitation that disrupted more than one-third of the quarter's available shipping days. Second quarter shipments declined less than 2%
notes: Strong demand (South Texas projects, energy recovery) and an all-time record June mitigated; cement plants near sold out can catch up. >33% of days disrupted vs a typical share perhaps ~15-20% (not stated) -> very low within-quarter elasticity (~0.05-0.1). Shows catch-up within a quarter when demand is strong.

weather_stated: precipitation days up 30% YoY; precipitation totals up ~40% YoY
deferred_or_lost: partly deferred (mgmt hopes 'some or most' recovered)
quote: we estimate that Houston alone accounted for approximately $6.5 million in lost or delayed EBITDA in the second quarter.
notes: Precip days +30% vs PRIOR YEAR (not normal). Houston weather cut company aggregates volume by 280bp (s52861702989635113722908); Houston ~10% of company EBITDA. If Houston is ~10% of aggregates volume, Houston's own volume fell ~25% on +30% rain days -> local elasticity ~0.9 within the quarter (rough, Houston volume share not stated). Also flooding and power outages. Mgmt: 'some or most of the lost volumes in markets like Houston can be recovered if we get a solid stretch of working days' (s51042537722381420200919).

weather_stated: record rainfall; rain days up 48% (MN) and 45% (IA) vs Q2 2023
quote: Weather in Minnesota and Iowa, two of our largest river markets, experienced record rainfall in the second quarter, with rain days up 48% and 45%, respectively, versus Q2 2023.
notes: Rain-day deviation vs prior year stated; cement organic volume decline not quantified in transcript and ~40% of the decline was lower imports (s89317976344146179493764). Useful region/period for weather lookup.

region: Houston, western/northern Florida, Carolinas, Georgia, Virginia
weather_stated: precipitation days up 20% YoY in footprint (85% of MSAs); precipitation totals up 65% vs Q3 2023
quote: In our footprint, precipitation days increased in 85% of our MSAs, and precipitation days were up 20% year-on-year. Precipitation totals were up 65% versus Q3 2023... we estimate the three discrete weather events cited amounted to approximately $15 million in foregone EBITDA
notes: Hurricanes Beryl, Debby, Helene (discrete events, incl. a flooded quarry: 120k tons cement, $12M of the $15M). Cumulative 2024 weather EBITDA headwind >$20M on ~$985M guided EBITDA (~2%). Mgmt: 'When we have good weather days, that's where we're recouping' (s326367888316420263175).

region: Central segment: Minnesota, South Dakota, Iowa, Texas
weather_stated: wet June with heavy rainfall
quote: Revenue decreased 7% for the quarter, largely related to weather, as this segment had a wet June, with heavy rainfall in parts of Minnesota, South Dakota, Iowa, and Texas.
notes: YoY change attributed 'largely' to weather; essentially one wet month. Mgmt: 'some of that work has certainly been delayed' (s348891632818438290190).

region: Central segment, pockets of Montana and Wyoming
weather_stated: it rained on nearly 40% of the available workdays in key markets
deferred_or_lost: partly deferred (backlog); mgmt expects to recapture pre-production costs in H2
quote: Rain plagued our operations throughout the Central segment and pockets of Montana and Wyoming. In key markets across those regions, it rained on nearly 40% of the available workdays, impacting revenue volumes and gross profit.
notes: Contracting services revenue -8.5%, asphalt volume -9% (s56271523270830602811657), but mixed with weak Oregon economy (Oregon aggregates -25%). Full-year EBITDA guide cut $55M midpoint, ~75% from H1 Oregon + wet weather (s47732897123388580663056) - not split. Rain on ~40% of workdays; a normal share is not given (lookup needed). CFO: lower volumes on fixed costs raised unit cost.

region: Southeast US (all ROAD states: AL, FL, GA, NC, SC, TN)
weather_stated: precipitation up ~30% vs typical Jul-Sep in each state; 7-9 additional workdays lost vs normal
deferred_or_lost: deferred (revenue moves to next quarter; margin lost)
quote: In each of our states, precipitation was up approximately 30% from July to September compared to typical rainfall levels for these months. This weather significantly impacted our Q4 and delayed approximately $30 million-$35 million of revenue into next year.
notes: $32.5M midpoint vs record Q4 revenue $279M (s333283507879230888219) -> 32.5/311.5 = -10.4%. Deviation is RAINFALL vs normal (+30%), elasticity on rainfall ~0.35. On days: 8 extra lost workdays of ~64 in the quarter = 12.5% of workdays -> revenue lost ~0.8x share of workdays lost. Deferred: 'This business is not lost, but rather moves forward'. Profit: FY adj. EBITDA margin fell to 9.9% from 12.5%, partly from lost fixed-cost recovery in Q4 (s249455415396197512105).

weather_stated: 30% abnormal precipitation increase
quote: excessive loss of workdays in the fourth quarter due to the 30% abnormal precipitation increase does hurt fixed cost recovery and absorption of our fleet and asphalt plants. While the revenue moves forward and is not lost, margins are impacted by extremely wet weather.
notes: Key deferred-vs-lost statement: revenue is deferred, but fixed-cost recovery on idle days is permanently lost. Margin effect mixed with inflation, not split.

weather_stated: precipitation 30% higher than normal (130% of normal) around asphalt plants
quote: there was a report that said in our local markets, when measuring around each of our asphalt plants, that the precipitation was 30% higher than normal or 130% of normal... We can't quantify exactly how much that is
notes: Unquantified revenue effect; record revenue and gross margin >15% anyway. Useful for lookup.

weather_stated: inclement weather two-thirds of the quarter; above-average precipitation in November and December
quote: These weather impacts show up mainly in fixed cost recovery at our plants and fleet and create extra project costs. We approximate an abnormal weather impact in Q1 of approximately $4 million.
notes: Profit-only estimate; Dec partly outside Mar-Nov window. Mgmt: 'over the course of a full year, the weather tends to even out' (prior-year dry Q1 over-recovered fixed assets).

weather_stated: more rain days than anticipated
quote: we did incur more rain days than we had anticipated. As Charles mentioned, that revenue does not go away, and the margins on those projects is not changed. That work is simply pushed forward into future periods.
notes: Unquantified; deferral statement. Q4 revenue +15% but gross profit -1%.

period_affected: FY2022 Q4 (Jul-Sep 2022, last week of Sep)
region: US East Coast, Florida to Boston (Hurricane Ian)
weather_stated: Hurricane Ian and significant rainfall across the East Coast during the last week of September
deferred_or_lost: ancillary installs lost/deferred; offset by later hurricane repair work
quote: Hurricane Ian and significant rainfall across the East Coast during the last week of September impacted our higher-margin ancillary services. Excluding this impact, Land Maintenance organic growth would have been about 3%
notes: Organic growth 2.2% actual vs ~3% ex-weather -> ~-0.8pt of maintenance revenue from ~1 week of rain. EBITDA hit ~$3M incl. hurricane prep costs (s52824697528709916215358) on Q4 adj. EBITDA $91M -> ~-3.2% of EBITDA: profit hit ~4x revenue hit because ancillary is high-margin. Contract maintenance revenue barely moves; weather hits ancillary (enhancements, installs).

quote: we're doing work to try to have our employees work four 10-hour days... if one day during the work week, Monday through Thursday, we get rain for the day that we can't work, we can have a makeup day on Friday. The employees still get their 40 hours.
notes: Unquantified; shows a single rain day is recovered within the week for contract maintenance (and crew pay), i.e. near-zero loss from scattered rain days. Relevant to trades_worker too.

region: Midwest and Great Plains cement markets
weather_stated: record rainfall; key markets 250% of historical average rainfall (November)
quote: We generated near-record third quarter revenue despite cement volumes being down 7% because of record rainfall in some areas. In key markets, rainfall reached 250% of historical averages.
notes: Deviation is RAINFALL (+150% vs normal) in key markets, not rain days, and only in part of the footprint/quarter. Elasticity on rainfall ~0.05; on rain days likely higher. Heavy materials operating earnings -20% but includes ~$8M planned maintenance. Eagle repeatedly: 'wet weather does not imply demand destruction. It just means interruption and delay.'

weather_stated: tremendous amount of wet weather across almost every market over 5-6 quarters, then a dry summer
quote: we've seen a tremendous amount of wet weather across almost every one of our markets. As we've been talking about, what ends up happening in those situations is projects don't get canceled, they just get delayed. They get pushed out.
notes: Unquantified deferral evidence; dry summer/fall 2019 recovered delayed projects. Also: 'It's been wet for so long that these jobs do drag out. You eventually pick them up.' (s199821431408042752409)

weather_stated: unusually wet weather; May and early June extremely wet; Midwest flooding
quote: Operating earnings were off 5% due to increased freight costs and unusually wet weather, which hampered the contributions from our concrete and aggregates in particular.
notes: Heavy materials revenue still +3%, cement volume +3%; earnings -5% from freight + weather (not split). Shows profit falling while revenue rose: under-absorption/logistics.

period_affected: FY2022 Q1 (Oct-Dec 2021): catch-up of Jul-Sep 2021 rain delay
weather_stated: favorable weather in the quarter
quote: we did have a lot of weather in the fourth quarter, and that revenue, as we said then, moved into the first quarter. We did have good first quarter, and we had good weather.
notes: Confirms the $30-35M delayed in Jul-Sep 2021 was recovered in Oct-Dec 2021 (analyst: 'you got all that back in December'; record $285M revenue, first time Q1 exceeded Q4 in company history, s85082705745793526295743). impact_usd is the recovered (positive) amount, midpoint. Season-level revenue loss ~0; the lost fixed-cost recovery was not recovered.

weather_stated: unusually wet weather across many markets in May
quote: Obviously, when it rains, we cannot work, when it's wet... Those days that we miss do create the need to be more productive to make up because our customers still want their projects delivered. When it rains, during the one day, we might make up for it on the weekend.
notes: Unquantified. Crews' rain-lost days are partly made up on weekends -> an hourly field worker recovers some lost pay; a day laborer with no weekend makeup does not.

region: Mid-Atlantic, Carolinas, Georgia; Colorado (wettest June on record)
weather_stated: second half of June a washout, rained nearly every day; Colorado wettest June on record
quote: One, relative to volume, we think in the quarter, we lost about one million tons simply due to weather. If you were here in the Mid-Atlantic, what you saw is the second half of June was frankly, a washout. It rained nearly every day.
notes: ~1M tons lost; Q2 2023 aggregates shipments fell 5.7% YoY (10-Q) but quarterly tonnage not found in the sources read, so % not computed (MLM ships 'modestly over 210 million tons' a year per s307208077365660732190 -> 1M is roughly 2% of a ~52M-ton quarter; rough). Colorado wettest June on record (s269458706378310302543).

period_affected: 2019 full year (2018 weather-deferred projects shipped in 2019)
quote: Our cement operations established new full-year records for volumes and gross profits. Shipments increased 10% to nearly 3.9 million tons, driven by robust Texas demand, 2018 weather-deferred projects, and an expanded distribution terminal footprint.
notes: Evidence that wet-2018 Texas work (record Sep/Oct 2018 rain) shipped in 2019, i.e. deferred across the year boundary rather than lost. Q3 2019 call: cement +21% record quarter 'driven by healthy Texas demand as well as weather deferred projects from earlier in the year' (s232614431203756489583).

weather_stated: 57% more weather-impacted days in Q4; 30% more for the full year (vs 2018)
quote: If we're looking at Colorado all by itself, asphalt and paving had 57% more weather impacted days in Q4. By the way, they had 30% more full-year impacted days.
notes: Weather-impacted DAYS +30% YoY for the year, yet Colorado asphalt shipments still +7.5% for 2019 with 'a notable portion' of backlog deferred into 2020 (s88517369884341128295731); asphalt margins disappointed mainly on weather (s59117627237842545897536). Shows days lost hit margin more than annual volume.

weather_stated: 45 days of rain and record accumulation
quote: Salt Lake City has had, as I mentioned in my comments, 45 days of rain and record accumulation. That particular market is 60% gross margin, and we were down 40% in volume.
notes: CAUTION: Jan-Mar (mostly outside the Mar-Nov rain_work window) and mixes record snow ('accumulation') with rain; market also had soft residential demand. Shows a single local market can lose ~40% of a quarter's volume when nearly every day is wet.

weather_stated: historically wet and slow start to the year (California atmospheric rivers)
deferred_or_lost: deferred and recovered later in the year
quote: the California Group's significant year-over-year revenue increase was in line with our expectations as the group overcame a historically wet and slow start to the year.
notes: California Group revenue +21% YoY in Q3 2023 (same paragraph). Catch-up evidence. Q1 2023: 'many locations from Southern California through Central California collected more than 150% abnormal rainfall totals' (s194844973828466485673). Q2 2023: emergency work only ~$50M vs $100M hoped and a few projects 'pushed to the right' (s317734348171718207843): some slippage into later periods. Q4 2023: strong second half since 'first half of the year was delayed due to the wet weather' (s275308242941953310483).

weather_stated: excessive rainfall; very wet April and especially May
quote: excessive rainfall in Texas, our largest exposure, and along the Gulf Coast, reduced segment adjusted EBITDA by approximately $3 million-$4 million in the quarter. Construction activity returned to healthy levels in June once the weather improved.
notes: Midpoint $3.5M. Segment EBITDA margin fell to 22.1% from 26% (also diesel). CEO 2024: 'it's not easy to ramp up a project and do it faster just because you were held up with rain' and plant fixed costs continue during shutdowns (s348730437757299942543).

weather_stated: first half very, very wet in Dallas
deferred_or_lost: partly lost (projects cannot be built faster)
quote: many times projects, it's not like they can build the road faster. So sometimes you see some additional demand that gets held up by weather... it's not easy to ramp up a project and do it faster just because you were held up with rain. So I would say, and remember, the rain has two impacts.
notes: Unquantified; argues catch-up is limited by project pace (deferral stretches into later periods rather than compressing), and plant costs continue while shut down.

period_affected: 2020 Q1 rain -> made up in Q2 2020
weather_stated: rain in Q1 2020
quote: They had a little bit of tailwinds from some work that was pushed out of the first quarter with rain that they were able to make that up, plus do what they anticipated in the second quarter.
notes: Unquantified catch-up evidence; site-development work with 'more makeup capacity' (s340444321170565861910).

region: Texas, New England, Midwest (8 of 11 regions wetter)
weather_stated: increased rain during May and June vs prior year in 8 of 11 regions
deferred_or_lost: partly lost (customers labor-constrained, cannot make up work short-term)
quote: Keep in mind that we are operating in a very labor-constrained market, and so the amount of dry days will continue to have an impact on our organic sales, given the inability of our customers to make up the work in the short term.
notes: Organic daily sales +1% vs April +5% and mid-single-digit in normal-weather South; wet regions flat to slightly negative -> ~-4 to -5pts vs underlying (my estimate; analyst suggested 'mid-single digit weather impact'). May flat-to-negative, June flat (s59645003342488013012140). EBITDA shortfall ~$4-5M on $114M adj. EBITDA (~-4%, s65732224036549111972287): profit fell about in line with sales. SiteOne sales proxy landscaper activity.

weather_stated: nine of 11 regions had fewer rain days in Q3 2019 than Q3 2018
quote: Landscaping product sales benefited from favorable weather and strong demand due in part from the backlog of work resulting from the challenging weather we had in the first half of the year. In a reversal of last quarter's result, nine of 11 geographic regions had fewer rain days
notes: Landscaping products +8% in Q3 vs +1% in Q2 and +4% YTD: part of the spring loss came back in summer. Q2 2019 CFO: high end of guidance 'will require a complete recovery, which we haven't, of the sales volume that was missed' (s65732224036549111972287).

weather_stated: Texas 11 more rain days than last year; Carolinas 12 more rain days (September); Hurricane Florence
quote: Just to describe September, we had Hurricane Florence that hit us, we also had wet weather really from Texas all the way up through to New Jersey for the month of September. If you look at the stats, Texas had 11 more rain days than last year. The Carolinas, 12 more rain days.
notes: Sep organic growth 3% vs ~5% quarter average and an expected strong fall season -> ~-2pts (my reading). +11/+12 rain days in a ~20-workday month = most days wet in those states, yet company-level hit is small (geographic diversification + distributor). CEO: Atlanta customers told to 'wait till spring of next year'; 'we would expect a lot of that work to carry into 2019' (s210832713881926588927).

weather_stated: wet weather in April and May after unusually favorable Q1
quote: Essentially, the weather, as we mentioned, it moves demand around... we really do not feel like we've lost any applications or we've lost any business for the year. It really has just been a shell game between quarters.
notes: Unquantified; management view that annual landscape demand is mostly unchanged by spring rain timing. Q2 2016: wet April-May hit sales, 'good recovery in organic sales, however, in June' (s235252332296201370844).

region: Northern markets, Pacific Northwest to East Coast
weather_stated: 7 of 9 regions, incl. all northern markets, had more rain in Q2 2022 than a very dry Q2 2021; late spring
quote: the combination of the wet weather and a late spring resulted in some lawn care operators reducing rounds of agronomic product applications.
notes: Northern markets 0% organic vs Sunbelt +17% (s244827851768181667730) but northern markets also faced a 24% comp and fertilizer price inflation; not a clean weather estimate. Skipped application rounds are a LOST (not deferred) service.

quote: Things that we put in this past year, like PTO, have been a huge benefit for our employees that when we get rain days or when there's a sick day they need to take.
notes: Unquantified. Large employers now cushion crew pay on rain days (PTO, 4x10 schedules with Friday makeup, s206150779179171940747). A salaried/PTO crew member loses little; an independent day laborer bears the full lost day.
